subject: why risking 1 percent per trade keeps your account alive
title: The 1% Rule That Keeps Traders Alive
hook: Most traders blow up over one number, not their strategy.
script: Most traders blow up over one number, not their strategy. Here it is: never risk more than one percent of your account on a single trade. On a ten thousand dollar account, that's a hundred dollars at risk. Lose ten in a row and you're still down only ten percent, fully able to recover. Risk ten percent each time instead, and a few bad trades wipe you out. Survival comes first. Big returns mean nothing if you're not around for them. Save this before your next trade.

subject: the position sizing formula that separates trading from gambling
title: Position Sizing: Are You Trading or Gambling?
hook: Skip this one formula and you're gambling, not trading.
script: Skip this one formula and you're gambling, not trading. Position size equals your dollar risk divided by your stop distance. Say you'll risk a hundred dollars and your stop sits two dollars below entry. A hundred divided by two is fifty shares. That's your size, no guessing. Most beginners pick a random number of shares and hope. Pros let the math decide before they ever click buy. The size protects you, not the prediction. Save this formula and run it on your next idea.

subject: how revenge trading quietly destroys trading accounts
title: Revenge Trading: The Habit That Empties Accounts
hook: One habit emptied my account faster than any bad trade.
script: One habit emptied my account faster than any bad trade. It's called revenge trading. You take a loss, your ego stings, so you jump straight back in to win it back. The next trade is bigger and angrier, and it loses too. Within an hour a hundred dollar slip becomes a thousand. The fix is boring but it works: set a daily loss limit, and after two losses, close the laptop. Walking away is a skill. The market opens again tomorrow. Save this so it never happens to you.

subject: why lifestyle creep makes you feel broke even on a higher salary
title: Why You Feel Broke on a Good Salary
hook: A raise to ninety thousand can leave you just as broke.
script: A raise to ninety thousand can leave you just as broke. Here's why. It's called lifestyle creep. Your income climbs, so the nicer apartment, the upgraded car, and the bigger plans climb right alongside it. You earn more but save the same, sometimes less. Someone on sixty thousand and someone on ninety can end the year with identical savings if every raise gets spent. The fix is simple: bank the next raise before you feel it arrive. Keep your costs flat while income grows. Save this and try it.

title: Do This Before You Invest a Single Dollar
hook: Don't invest a single dollar until these three things are done.
script: Don't invest a single dollar until these three things are done. One, build a small emergency fund, even one month of expenses, so a surprise bill doesn't force you to sell. Two, clear high interest debt, because a credit card charging twenty percent beats almost any return you'll earn. Three, know your time horizon, since money you need next year shouldn't ride the market. Investing on a shaky base is building on sand. Get the foundation right first. subject: what a long candlestick wick is actually telling you
title: What a Candle Wick Is Really Telling You
hook: That tiny wick on the candle is screaming a message.
script: That tiny wick on the candle is screaming a message most beginners ignore. A candle has a body and thin lines above and below called wicks. A long wick means price pushed hard in that direction, then got slapped back before the candle closed. That's rejection. A long wick on top says buyers tried to run higher and sellers shoved them down. It's a footprint of who lost the fight. One candle isn't proof on its own, but it tells a story. subject: what a doji candle reveals about market indecision
title: The Doji Candle: When the Market Can't Decide
hook: This skinny candle means buyers and sellers just tied.
script: This skinny candle means buyers and sellers just tied. It's called a doji, and it forms when price opens and closes at almost the exact same spot. Think of it as a tug of war where neither side moved the rope. Buyers pushed up, sellers pushed down, and they cancelled out. That's indecision. After a long strong run, a doji can hint the momentum is tiring, because the crowd suddenly hesitated. It's context, not a crystal ball. Follow for more candlestick basics explained simply.

subject: why trading without a stop loss is the costliest beginner mistake
title: Trading Without a Stop Loss Is a Slow Bankruptcy
hook: No stop loss is why one trade can erase fifty wins.
script: No stop loss is why one trade can erase fifty wins. A stop loss is the price where you agree to be wrong and get out. Skip it and a small loss has permission to become a giant one. Picture fifty good trades earning ten dollars each, then a single runaway loser drops five hundred. The math just undid weeks of work. Decide your exit before you enter, when you're calm, not while you're panicking and hoping it comes back. Hope is not a plan. Save this before your next trade.
